messages.content: I want to characterize when heterogeneous treatment effects remain partially identifiable with weak instruments and bounded exclusion violations in observational healthcare. What should that goal include?

It should address what can still be learned about differences in treatment effects when the instrument provides limited information and its exclusion restriction may fail within a stated bound. Two requirements are central: achieve at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes, and establish sharp identification bounds while characterizing when those bounds improve upon bounds obtained without instruments.
What does “partially identifiable” mean here?

It means the available assumptions and information may restrict a heterogeneous treatment effect to a range without determining a single value. The aim is to characterize that range and the conditions under which it remains informative, rather than presume that weak instruments and bounded exclusion violations permit point identification.
Why mention weak instruments and exclusion violations together?

They are distinct limitations on what an instrument can tell us. A weak instrument may carry little information relevant to treatment effects, while an exclusion violation allows some association outside the idealized exclusion restriction. The goal considers both at once: how much information remains when instrument strength is limited and exclusion violations are bounded, not necessarily zero.
Does a bounded exclusion violation mean we can treat exclusion as exact after all?

No. A bound limits the size of a permitted violation; it does not assert that the violation is zero. Any identification claim must respect the allowed violations. The goal does not specify a numerical bound or its particular mathematical form, so those details should not be assumed.
And “heterogeneous treatment effects” means we cannot just describe one overall effect?

Right. The focus is on how treatment effects differ, rather than only on a single overall treatment-effect summary. The stated goal does not choose a particular definition of heterogeneity or a particular subgroup, so the characterization should be understood at that level of generality.
How should I read the at-least-95% coverage requirement?

It is a requirement for the confidence sets, not a claim that coverage has already been demonstrated. “Uniformly” matters: the at-least-95% guarantee is intended to hold throughout the specified classes of instrument strength and exclusion violations, rather than only at one favorable configuration. The precise confidence-set target and the classes themselves would need to be specified before that guarantee could be assessed.
So coverage at a single fixed instrument strength would not, by itself, meet the requirement?

Correct. A calculation or argument for one fixed configuration would not by itself establish at least 95% coverage uniformly over the specified classes. The requirement includes the configurations covered by those classes, including the weak-instrument and permitted-exclusion-violation settings they specify.
What is meant by sharp identification bounds?

Sharp bounds describe exactly the values compatible with the stated information and assumptions: values outside the bounds are ruled out, and values inside are not ruled out on those grounds. Establishing sharpness is stronger than merely giving a valid, possibly wider range. It is an objective here, not a result that has already been established.
What are those bounds supposed to be compared against?

Against bounds obtained without instruments. The task is not merely to derive instrument-based bounds, but to characterize when using the instrument—while allowing for its weakness and bounded exclusion violations—actually improves on that no-instrument baseline.
Does “improves” mean the instrument-based bounds must always be narrower?

No. The wording asks *when* they improve, not for a blanket assertion that they always do. Conceptually, an improvement means the instrument rules out values that remain possible under the bounds without instruments. Whether that happens depends on the conditions being characterized; the stated goal does not supply those conditions or a conclusion about particular cases.
Could the instrument still matter even if it does not deliver a single treatment-effect value?

Yes. Partial identification allows an instrument to be informative without yielding a point estimate: it may narrow the compatible range. But whether it narrows the range relative to the no-instrument bounds is precisely something to establish, not something to assume.
Can you put the two requirements together without implying the work is already done?

The aim is to determine the sharp bounds on heterogeneous treatment effects in observational healthcare under weak instruments and bounded exclusion violations, and to characterize when those bounds are tighter than bounds without instruments. Alongside that identification analysis, the aim is to obtain confidence sets with at least 95% coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. Both are requirements to meet, not findings to report in advance.
How would you approach the sharp bounds and the coverage requirement together?

A proposed approach is to use stratified response-type linear programs that encode bounded exclusion violations, then project multinomial confidence regions through those programs. The linear programs would address the identification bounds for heterogeneous treatment effects; the projection would account for uncertainty in the observed information without relying on a strong instrument. The resulting bounds would also be benchmarked against bounds without instruments.
What does “stratified” contribute to that proposal?

It makes the treatment-effect heterogeneity explicit: bounds can be characterized within strata rather than only for a pooled effect. The proposal does not specify which strata to use. Whatever strata are specified, the bounds and the no-instrument comparison need to refer to the same treatment-effect targets.
And what is the role of response types?

Response types provide a way to represent possible underlying treatment and outcome responses while relating them to what is observed. In the proposed linear programs, their possible distributions would be constrained by the observed information and by the allowed exclusion violations. Optimizing the treatment-effect quantity over the compatible distributions yields candidate lower and upper bounds.
Why put bounded exclusion violations inside the linear programs rather than address them afterward?

Because the permitted violations affect which response-type distributions are compatible with the assumptions. Encoding those limits in the feasible set lets the bounds reflect the stated relaxation of exclusion. Applying a correction afterward would not, by itself, show that the resulting bounds describe exactly the compatible values.
Does solving a linear program automatically make its answer a sharp identification bound?

No. The proposed formulation would need to represent all and only the configurations permitted by the observed information and assumptions. If it does, its extrema can establish sharp bounds for the specified target. Merely obtaining numerical extrema from a linear program would not establish sharpness if its representation omitted compatible configurations or admitted incompatible ones.
How does the multinomial confidence-region part work conceptually?

Instead of treating observed proportions as if they were known without error, the proposal takes a confidence region for the relevant multinomial probabilities and projects that region into the treatment-effect bounds. Conceptually, it considers the effect values compatible with probabilities in the confidence region and with the response-type and bounded-exclusion constraints. This separates uncertainty about the observed probabilities from the partial identification that remains even if those probabilities were known.
Why would projection be safer when the instrument is weak?

The idea is not to obtain precision by dividing an estimated effect by a potentially tiny measure of instrument strength. Projection retains the configurations compatible with the confidence region, including weak-instrument configurations in the specified class. That makes it a candidate route to weak-IV-safe coverage, although the at-least-95% uniform coverage requirement would still need to be established for the confidence region and its projection.
If the multinomial region has 95% coverage, is that enough to say the final confidence set has at least 95% coverage?

It can support that conclusion if the region covers the relevant probability vector with at least 95% probability uniformly over the specified classes, the projection includes all treatment-effect values compatible with every probability vector in that region under the stated assumptions, and the true configuration belongs to those classes. Those conditions matter. The proposal alone does not demonstrate the uniform guarantee.
So the identification bounds and the projected confidence set are different objects?

Yes. For a given underlying distribution of observables, identification bounds describe which treatment-effect values remain compatible with the assumptions. A projected confidence set also reflects sampling uncertainty about that distribution. Keeping them distinct helps avoid mistaking a wide confidence set caused by limited data for a wide identification region—or the reverse.
Where does the no-IV benchmark enter?

It provides the comparison needed to assess the value of the instrument. The proposed analysis would compare the stratified bounded-exclusion bounds with bounds for the same treatment-effect targets obtained without instruments, then characterize the conditions under which the instrument-based bounds are tighter. Benchmarking does not presume that an instrument improves every bound.
Could a weak instrument still improve a bound under this approach?

That remains a question for the bounds and their comparison to answer. Weakness does not, on its own, establish either improvement or no improvement. The proposal is designed to let the compatible response-type configurations determine whether the instrument rules out effect values that the no-IV analysis leaves possible, while respecting bounded exclusion violations.
Does “weak-IV-safe coverage” mean the bounds will necessarily be narrow?

No. Coverage concerns whether the confidence set includes the relevant true treatment-effect value at the required rate; informativeness concerns how narrow the set or identification bounds are. A procedure can be designed to protect coverage under weak instruments while returning broad sets when the information is limited. The proposal seeks valid inference and sharp identification bounds, but neither property promises narrow bounds in every case.
What would need to be checked before calling this proposal successful?

The response-type linear programs would need to yield sharp bounds under the stated stratification and bounded-exclusion assumptions. The projected multinomial confidence regions would need to achieve at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. Finally, the no-IV benchmark would need to show exactly when the instrument-based bounds improve upon bounds without instruments. These are checks required by the goal, not results established by proposing the method.
Can you state the proposed workflow without turning it into a claim of findings?

For each specified stratum and treatment-effect target, formulate a response-type linear program incorporating the bounded exclusion violations and use it to seek sharp identification bounds. Project an appropriate multinomial confidence region through the resulting feasible configurations to seek weak-IV-safe confidence sets, then benchmark the identification bounds against no-IV bounds. The analysis would have to establish sharpness, at least 95% uniform coverage over the specified classes, and the conditions for improvement; none follows solely from naming the workflow.
For binary treatment and outcome, which first-stage differences and exclusion-violation limits yield narrower stratum-specific bounds than the no-IV bounds?

That is the question the proposed analysis needs to answer; no numerical threshold is specified yet. A first-stage difference describes how treatment probabilities differ across instrument values within a stratum. Whether a particular difference is enough to narrow the treatment-effect bounds also depends on the observed treatment–outcome probabilities and on how much exclusion violation is allowed. The response-type linear programs can characterize the combinations that produce an improvement, using the no-IV bounds for the same stratum-specific target as the benchmark.
Why can’t we give a cutoff based only on the first-stage difference?

Because the first stage describes only one aspect of the observed relationship. Identification bounds also depend on which treatment and outcome patterns are compatible with the observations and the permitted exclusion violations. Two configurations could have the same first-stage difference yet impose different restrictions on the stratum-specific effect. A cutoff based on instrument strength alone would therefore need additional conditions that have not been specified.
How should the exclusion-violation limit enter the comparison?

It belongs in the constraints defining which response types remain possible. For each specified limit, the bounded-exclusion linear program would give the compatible effect range, which could then be compared with the no-IV range. A more permissive limit can leave more configurations possible, but the question is whether the instrument still removes any effect values allowed by the no-IV analysis at that limit.
Is the question essentially asking for a boundary between informative and uninformative combinations?

Yes, provided “informative” is defined relative to the no-IV bounds. The desired characterization would distinguish combinations of first-stage differences and exclusion-violation limits for which the instrument-based stratum-specific bound is narrower from combinations for which it is not. It should not assume that this boundary is a single universal number shared by all strata and observed distributions.
What exactly counts as a narrower bound?

For an interval with lower and upper endpoints, one clear comparison is whether the instrument-based interval is a strict subset of the corresponding no-IV interval: its lower endpoint is higher, its upper endpoint is lower, or both, with neither endpoint moving outward. If “narrower” is meant specifically as a smaller interval width, that can be stated and checked as well. In either case, the comparison must use the same stratum-specific treatment-effect target and aligned maintained assumptions.
So it is possible for just one endpoint to improve?

That is one possibility the comparison should allow for. The question does not require both endpoints to move inward. Reporting which endpoint changes, as well as whether the overall interval becomes narrower, would make the characterization more precise without presuming that any particular improvement occurs.
Would a larger first-stage difference necessarily produce tighter bounds?

Not on the information given. If other observed probabilities also change, the compatible response types may change in ways that a first-stage difference alone does not capture. The proposed characterization should examine first-stage differences together with the exclusion-violation limits and the relevant observed distribution, rather than treating greater first-stage separation as an automatic guarantee of narrower bounds.
Would a smaller exclusion-violation limit necessarily help?

If limits are defined so that a smaller value permits a subset of the configurations allowed by a larger value, tightening that limit cannot enlarge the feasible set within the same formulation. But that does not, by itself, establish a strict improvement over the no-IV bounds. The bounds might remain unchanged, so the comparison still has to be made.
Does binary treatment and binary outcome make the answer straightforward?

It makes a response-type formulation more concrete, but it does not supply the missing thresholds. The question still requires a specified stratum, a definition of the first-stage difference being compared, a precise exclusion-violation constraint, and the observed probabilities used in the bounds. Binary treatment and outcome do not alone determine which combinations beat the no-IV benchmark.
How would you phrase the answer we are trying to obtain, without claiming we already have it?

For binary treatment and outcome, characterize, stratum by stratum, the combinations of first-stage differences and permitted exclusion-violation limits under which the sharp bounded-exclusion IV bounds are narrower than the corresponding no-IV bounds. The characterization should identify the comparison criterion and account for the other observed probabilities on which the bounds depend. No particular first-stage cutoff or violation limit can be asserted from the question alone.

I have a more specific hypothesis for the binary-treatment, binary-outcome question: within strata, first-stage differences ≥0.10 and exclusion caps ≤0.02 risk units reduce median bound width by ≥15% versus no-IV bounds. How should I state it without presenting it as a result?

State it explicitly as a hypothesis: “Within strata, we hypothesize that first-stage differences of at least 0.10, together with exclusion-violation caps of at most 0.02 risk units, yield a median bound width at least 15% smaller than the corresponding no-IV bound width.” That preserves the proposed thresholds, the within-stratum setting, and the no-IV comparison without claiming the reduction has been observed or established.
Is 0.10 a minimum first-stage difference or an exact value?
It is a minimum under the stated hypothesis: ≥0.10 includes 0.10 and larger first-stage differences. The hypothesis does not say that 0.10 is an established cutoff at which improvement begins.
And the exclusion cap goes in the opposite direction?

Yes. ≤0.02 risk units includes a cap of 0.02 risk units and smaller caps. It describes the hypothesized range of permitted exclusion violations; it does not say the actual violation equals 0.02 or that exclusion holds exactly.
What is the ≥15% referring to?

It refers to a relative reduction in median bound width compared with the no-IV benchmark, not a reduction of 15 risk units or necessarily a reduction in each individual bound. The comparison needs to use the corresponding treatment-effect target within the stratum.
Could I instead say the IV bounds are 15% narrower for every stratum?

That would be stronger than the stated hypothesis. The hypothesis says “within strata” and specifies a reduction in *median* bound width; it does not assert a ≥15% reduction for every bound or every stratum. Those distinctions should remain visible until the unit over which the median is calculated is specified.
Do these thresholds answer exactly which first stages and exclusion limits give narrower bounds?

Not yet. They propose a particular region—first-stage differences ≥0.10 and exclusion caps ≤0.02 risk units—and a particular anticipated improvement of ≥15% in median width versus no-IV. They do not establish that improvement, identify a necessary cutoff, or characterize all combinations that might yield narrower bounds.
Why keep “median” rather than simply saying bound width?

Because it is part of the hypothesis and changes the claim. A median summarizes a collection of bound widths; a statement about the median need not hold for every member of that collection. The hypothesis does not specify here exactly which collection is summarized, so that should be defined before evaluating it rather than silently replaced with a claim about every interval.
Does a cap of 0.02 risk units mean a 2% reduction in width?

No. The 0.02 risk units limits the permitted exclusion violation; it is not the bound-width reduction. If risk is expressed on a zero-to-one scale, 0.02 risk units corresponds to two percentage points of risk. The hypothesized reduction in median bound width is separately stated as at least 15% relative to no-IV.
Can I say that meeting both thresholds guarantees the 15% reduction?

No. “Guarantees” would turn an untested hypothesis into an established claim. Even when both threshold conditions hold, the bound comparison still has to be evaluated. The proposal is that the specified conditions are associated with that degree of median-width improvement, not that the improvement has already been proved for every compatible configuration.
How does this relate to sharp bounds?

The width comparison is meaningful for the proposed identification analysis if the bounds being compared are defined for the same stratum-specific effect and the instrument-based bounds are established as sharp under their stated constraints. But the numerical hypothesis about a ≥15% median-width reduction does not itself establish sharpness; that remains a separate requirement.
Does the 15% hypothesis say anything about at least 95% confidence-set coverage?

No. Bound width concerns informativeness, whereas the at-least-95% requirement concerns confidence-set coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. A hypothesis about narrower median identification bounds cannot substitute for a coverage argument.
What is the most careful one-sentence version, then?

“We hypothesize that, within strata, first-stage differences ≥0.10 combined with exclusion-violation caps ≤0.02 risk units reduce median bound width by ≥15% relative to corresponding no-IV bounds.” It presents the numerical claim as a hypothesis and leaves its evaluation open.
How can we evaluate the hypothesis about narrower bounds?

The proposed activity is to simulate 10,000 binary-outcome datasets over grids spanning first-stage differences from 0 to 0.20 and exclusion caps from 0 to 0.05, then compare median linear-program (LP) bound widths with median no-IV bound widths and examine coverage. This is an evaluation plan, not a report of simulated results.
Does that grid include the hypothesized region?

Yes. First-stage differences ≥0.10 and exclusion caps ≤0.02 risk units fall within the stated ranges. The ranges alone do not specify the grid points or their spacing, though, so they do not by themselves say exactly which threshold combinations will be simulated.
What does the median-width comparison test?

It addresses the hypothesis that, within strata, the specified first-stage and exclusion-cap conditions reduce median bound width by at least 15% relative to no-IV bounds. The comparison should keep the stratum-specific treatment-effect target aligned between the LP and no-IV bounds. No width reduction has yet been observed or established by stating the simulation plan.
Is the 0.05 upper end of the exclusion-cap grid itself a claim that bounds improve there?

No. It is the upper end of the range proposed for evaluation, not a claimed improvement threshold. Comparing widths across the range can show how the bounds behave under different permitted exclusion violations without presupposing that the LP bounds beat the no-IV bounds at every cap.
What should coverage refer to in this comparison?

Coverage concerns whether the confidence set contains the relevant treatment-effect value, rather than how wide the identification bounds are. In the proposed approach, that would mean examining coverage of confidence sets obtained by projecting multinomial confidence regions, alongside the LP/no-IV width comparison. The activity does not report a coverage rate.
If the simulation shows coverage above 95%, would that establish the uniform requirement?

Not by itself. Simulated coverage can provide evidence about the configurations examined, but the requirement is at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. A finite grid and 10,000 simulated datasets cannot alone establish a guarantee for every configuration in those classes.
Could we treat the 10,000 datasets as 10,000 for every combination on the grid?

The activity says to simulate 10,000 binary-outcome datasets *over* the grids; it does not specify how those datasets are allocated among grid combinations. Calling it 10,000 per combination would add a detail that is not stated.
Should the median LP/no-IV comparison and the coverage check be combined into one success measure?

They should remain distinct checks. The median-width comparison evaluates informativeness relative to no-IV bounds, including the proposed ≥15% reduction in the hypothesized region. The coverage check evaluates the inferential behavior of the confidence sets. Narrower bounds do not themselves demonstrate coverage, and coverage does not establish that the LP bounds are narrower.
Would these simulations establish that the LP bounds are sharp?

No. The simulations can compare widths and examine coverage behavior over the stated grids. Sharpness requires showing that the LP bounds exactly characterize the effect values compatible with the assumptions and observed information. That requirement cannot be replaced by a favorable simulated width comparison.
So what can we say now about the outcome of this activity?

Only what is proposed: simulate 10,000 binary-outcome datasets over first-stage differences of 0–0.20 and exclusion caps of 0–0.05, and compare median LP and no-IV bound widths as well as coverage. The plan is designed to evaluate the stated width hypothesis and inspect coverage across the simulated configurations; it supplies no results yet.
What did the comparison show for the specified first-stage and exclusion-cap region?

At first-stage differences ≥0.10 and exclusion caps ≤0.02 risk units, median LP bound widths were 19% narrower than the corresponding no-IV widths. That is a result about median width in the stated region, not a claim that every individual bound narrowed by 19%.
What did the coverage check show?
The minimum coverage observed across the evaluated grid was 95.1%. “Gridwide minimum” means that 95.1% was the lowest coverage reported among the grid configurations, not an average across them.
Does the 95.1% figure apply only to the region where the LP widths were narrower?

No. The width result is stated for first-stage differences ≥0.10 and exclusion caps ≤0.02. The 95.1% figure is stated as the minimum coverage across the grid as a whole. They describe different scopes of the evaluation.
Can I say that every confidence set covered its target?

No. A coverage rate describes how often a confidence set contains its target across repetitions; it does not say that every individual set covered. The reported figure is a gridwide minimum coverage rate of 95.1%, not universal coverage of individual sets.
What does “19% narrower” use as its reference?

The reference is the no-IV bound width. The reported comparison is between median LP widths and the corresponding no-IV widths in the specified region. It is a relative width comparison, not a reduction of 19 risk units.
Does that tell us both endpoints of each LP bound moved inward?

No. A median-width result does not identify how the lower and upper endpoints moved, or say that every interval became narrower. Endpoint behavior would require a separate comparison that is not reported here.
Should I describe ≥0.10 and ≤0.02 as exact cutoffs for when instruments help?

No. The result reports narrowing in that specified region. It does not establish that 0.10 is the smallest first-stage difference that can yield narrower bounds, that 0.02 risk units is the largest useful exclusion cap, or that improvement cannot occur elsewhere.
Does the gridwide coverage result establish at least 95% coverage uniformly over the full specified classes?

It reports a minimum of 95.1% on the evaluated grid. That empirical result should not be recast as a uniform coverage guarantee over every configuration in the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. A gridwide observation and a uniform guarantee have different scopes.
And does the narrower-width result establish that the LP bounds are sharp?

Not by itself. The reported 19% compares widths with no-IV bounds. Sharpness is a separate claim about whether the LP bounds exactly capture the effect values compatible with the stated information and assumptions; neither the width comparison nor the coverage figure alone establishes it.
How can I report both findings in one sentence without overstating them?

“For first-stage differences ≥0.10 and exclusion caps ≤0.02 risk units, median LP bound widths were 19% narrower than no-IV bound widths; the minimum observed coverage across the evaluated grid was 95.1%.” This keeps the width result tied to its specified region and the coverage result tied to the grid.
Given the 19% narrowing and the simulated 95.1% minimum coverage, what should we decide about the stratified LP bounds?

Advance the stratified LP bounds on the basis of the reported 19% narrowing in median width relative to no-IV bounds, but require a uniform-coverage proof beyond the simulated 95.1% gridwide minimum. The width result provides a reason to continue with the approach; the simulated coverage result does not, by itself, establish the required coverage guarantee.
What does “advance” mean in this decision?

It means continue developing the stratified LP bounds rather than treating the approach as finished. The decision is favorable to pursuing the bounds because of the observed width improvement, while explicitly reserving the coverage claim until a uniform proof is available.
Is the 19% figure a claim about every stratum-specific interval?

No. It is the reported reduction in median LP bound width versus no-IV in the evaluated region. Using that result to advance the approach does not turn it into a claim that every interval, or every stratum, narrowed by 19%.
Why isn't a gridwide minimum of 95.1% enough for the coverage requirement?

Because it is a simulated minimum over evaluated grid configurations. The requirement is at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. A minimum observed on a finite grid does not establish what happens at every configuration in those classes, so the decision calls for a proof beyond the simulation.
Could I write that coverage has been validated at 95.1%?

That wording would be too broad without qualification. You can say the minimum simulated coverage across the evaluated grid was 95.1%. You should not present that number as a proved uniform coverage rate or as completion of the at-least-95% uniform-coverage requirement.
Does requiring a proof mean we disregard the simulated coverage result?

No. The 95.1% gridwide minimum remains an observation from the simulation. The decision distinguishes its role from that of a proof: it can inform the assessment of the approach on the evaluated grid, but it cannot replace a uniform guarantee over the specified classes.
Are the width improvement and coverage proof testing the same thing?

No. The 19% narrowing concerns how informative the LP bounds were relative to no-IV bounds in the reported comparison. Uniform coverage concerns whether the confidence sets attain the required at-least-95% coverage throughout the specified classes. The decision uses the first result as a reason to advance the bounds and keeps the second requirement open.
Should the decision say that the stratified LP bounds are already sharp?

Not on the strength of these numbers alone. A median-width comparison and a simulated coverage minimum do not establish sharpness. The decision is to advance the stratified LP bounds while requiring a uniform-coverage proof; it should not add a finding about sharpness that the decision does not state.
Does the decision specify how to prove uniform coverage?

No. It specifies that a proof is required beyond the simulated 95.1% minimum, but does not prescribe the proof's form or claim that one has been completed. Any argument offered would need to address coverage uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes, rather than only the simulated grid.
So is the 95.1% minimum the reason to advance, or is the 19% narrowing the reason?

The decision expressly bases advancement of the stratified LP bounds on the 19% narrowing. It separately notes the simulated 95.1% minimum as insufficient for a uniform-coverage claim and requires a proof. Those are complementary parts of the decision, not interchangeable justifications.
Would “advance subject to proof” capture the distinction?

Yes, if you keep both the reason and the outstanding requirement explicit: advance the stratified LP bounds based on the reported 19% median-width narrowing versus no-IV, while requiring a proof of uniform at-least-95% coverage beyond the simulated 95.1% gridwide minimum. “Subject to proof” should not imply that the proof already exists.
Can we call the simulated 95.1% minimum a uniform result over the grid?

You can say it is the minimum *observed across the evaluated grid*. Calling it a uniform result without that qualifier risks confusing the finite-grid simulation with the required uniform coverage guarantee over the specified classes. The decision deliberately keeps those two claims separate.
What is the shortest faithful statement of the decision?
Advance stratified LP bounds based on 19% median-width narrowing versus no-IV, but require a uniform-coverage proof beyond the simulated 95.1% gridwide minimum.
What is the plan for the adopted stratified LPs?

Prove that their identification bounds are sharp, prove uniform confidence-set coverage of at least 95% through exact multinomial projection, and map the instrument-strength and exclusion-violation regions in which the bounds improve on corresponding no-IV bounds. These are tasks to carry out, not claims that the proofs or map are complete.
What would a sharpness proof need to show?

For each specified stratum and treatment-effect target, it would need to show that the LP bounds include every value compatible with the observed information and the bounded-exclusion assumptions, while excluding values that are incompatible. In particular, the endpoints must be attainable under the stated model, rather than merely being conservative limits produced by the formulation.
Is solving each LP enough to prove that?

No. Solving the optimization problem gives extrema over its encoded feasible set. A sharpness proof must also justify that the feasible set faithfully represents the response-type configurations allowed by the assumptions and the observed information. Otherwise, even a correctly solved LP could give bounds that are too wide or too narrow for the intended model.
How does the proof account for heterogeneous treatment effects?

It must apply to the treatment-effect target defined within each stratum, not just to an overall effect. The strata and their targets need to be specified so that compatibility, endpoint attainability, and the later no-IV comparison all refer to the same quantities. The plan does not prescribe particular healthcare strata.
What is meant by exact multinomial projection in the coverage part?

The plan is to start with a confidence region for the relevant multinomial probabilities whose coverage can be justified exactly, then project all probabilities in that region through the stratified LP constraints into a confidence set for the treatment-effect target. Projection retains the effect values compatible with probabilities admitted by the region and with the bounded-exclusion model. The required proof would connect coverage of the multinomial region to coverage of that projected set.
Does “exact” mean the treatment effect becomes exactly identified?

No. It refers to the proposed basis for the coverage argument, not to point identification of the treatment effect. The projected confidence set may remain broad because sampling uncertainty and partial identification are different sources of uncertainty. Sharp bounds can still form an interval rather than a single value.
Why project the whole multinomial region instead of plugging in the observed proportions?

Plugging in observed proportions treats them as though they were known exactly. Projecting the confidence region allows for their sampling uncertainty: it considers the treatment-effect values compatible with the probability vectors the region admits. That is the proposed route to a confidence set whose coverage can be established even across the specified weak-instrument settings.
What does the uniform part of the proof require?

The proof must establish at least 95% confidence-set coverage throughout the specified classes of instrument strength and exclusion violations, not merely at selected configurations. It must also show that the projection argument remains valid for the treatment-effect target throughout those classes. The plan does not state the classes' precise boundaries or assert that such a proof has already been obtained.
Would an exact multinomial confidence region automatically finish that proof?

Not without the remaining links. Its coverage must hold over the relevant multinomial distributions in the specified classes, and the projected set must include every target value compatible with a covered true probability vector under the stated LP constraints. The plan is to establish those links, rather than infer the final guarantee from the word “exact” alone.
Does the coverage proof also establish sharpness?

They are separate proof obligations. Coverage concerns how often a confidence set contains its target under repeated sampling. Sharpness concerns whether the identification bounds exactly characterize the effect values compatible with the model for a given observable distribution. Exact multinomial projection is the proposed coverage route; the stratified LP formulation still needs its own sharpness justification.
What does it mean to map strength–violation regions?

It means characterize combinations of instrument strength and permitted exclusion violation according to whether the stratified LP bounds improve on the corresponding bounds without instruments. The resulting map should say where an improvement occurs under the stated assumptions and comparison criterion, rather than suggest that an instrument helps equally under every combination.
Is that map just a list of first-stage values?

No. Instrument strength is one dimension, and the permitted exclusion violation is another. The bound comparison can also depend on the relevant observed distribution and stratum-specific target. A faithful map needs to make its conditions clear rather than imply that instrument strength alone determines whether the no-IV bounds improve.
What does “improve no-IV bounds” mean in the map?

It means the instrument-based LP bounds rule out treatment-effect values that remain compatible with the corresponding no-IV analysis. The comparison must concern the same stratum-specific target and make clear what criterion is being used—for example, a strictly narrower identification interval. The plan calls for characterizing the improvement regions; it does not state their boundaries.
Could the map show regions with no improvement?

Yes. To characterize *where* the LP bounds improve on no-IV bounds, it is also useful to distinguish combinations where they do not. The plan does not predetermine which combinations fall on either side or claim that all weak instruments are uninformative.
Are the proof and the map intended to answer different parts of the overall question?

They are complementary. Sharpness establishes that the reported identification bounds are the bounds implied by the specified model. Uniform at-least-95% coverage establishes the required inferential guarantee for confidence sets. The strength–violation map characterizes when using the instrument improves identification relative to no-IV bounds. None of those tasks substitutes for the others.
What should we avoid claiming while this is still a plan?

Avoid saying that the adopted LPs have already been proved sharp, that exact multinomial projection has already delivered uniform ≥95% coverage, or that the boundaries of the improvement regions have been established.
